text: The law; the law of Moses.

title: Nehemiah 8:6
text: Proper attention to the word of God will lead a people to bless him for his goodness, and to worship him in the way of his appointment.

title: Nehemiah 8:8
text: Gave the sense--caused them to understand; this may mean simply that they expounded to the people the meaning of what was read.  But as it is certain that soon after the captivity the old Hebrew ceased to be a living language among the Jews, and the Aramaen or Chaldee took its place, it is probable that for this reason all but the better educated among the Jews needed an interpretation of what was read.

title: Nehemiah 8:9
text:
Tirshatha; governor. 
 
  The people wept; in view of their transgressions and the punishment which they deserved. 
 
Sorrow for sin, however great or long continued, should never prevent humble trust in God, or hinder any from using the bounties of Providence with cheerful gratitude, and imparting liberally to those who are destitute, that all may rejoice together.

title: Nehemiah 8:13
text: Due attention to the word of God will lead men to have respect to all his commandments; nor will attention to one set of duties prevent them from promptly engaging in and faithfully performing others to which they are called.

title: Nehemiah 8:14
text: In the feast of the seventh month; the feast of tabernacles.  Leviticus 23:34

title: Nehemiah 8:17
text:
Made booths; in remembrance of their fathers' having dwelt in tents forty years in the wilderness. 
 
  There was very great gladness; in view of their being settled again in Canaan, as there was in the days of Joshua, when they took possession of it. 
 
Readiness to engage in all known duty, and fidelity in the performance of it, fill the soul with gladness; and through grace prepare it to rejoice for ever with joy unspeakable and full of glory.

title: Nehemiah 8:18
text: According unto the manner; as prescribed in th law of Moses.

title: Nehemiah 9:1
text: This month; Tishri, the seventh month.

title: Nehemiah 9:3
text: Due attention to the word of God will lead to humble confession of sin, and hearty devotion to his worship and service.

title: Nehemiah 9:5
text: Though the Lord is exalted above all human conception, yet he is pleased with the praises of his people, and glorified by all who worship him in spirit and in truth.

title: Nehemiah 9:8
text: God is faithful to his promises, and never disappoints the well-grounded hopes of those who trust in him.

title: Nehemiah 9:13
text:
Judgments; especially judicial decisions. 
 
  Statutes; what he ordained. 
 
The laws of Jehovah are all right and good; and suited to promote not only his glory, but the excellence, usefulness, and happiness of all who obey them.   Romans 7:12 Galatians 5:14 Galatians 5:22 Galatians 5:23

title: Nehemiah 9:16
text: No mercies are so numerous, great, or long continued as to lead men, without the grace of God, to obey him; but the greater and more constant their mercies, the greater will be their ingratitude, till they ripen for ruin.

title: Nehemiah 9:17
text: Appointed a captain; resolved to do it.   Numbers 14:1-4

title: Nehemiah 9:20
text:
Thy good Spirit to instruct them; by the mouth of his servants.  Nehemiah 9:30  
 
The Lord, by his Spirit, often admonishes and instructs even the most rebellious; and for a long time waits to be gracious, doing them good and using all suitable means to lead them to their own destruction.

title: Nehemiah 9:24
text: Children who inherit great blessings through the instrumentality of their parents and others, not unfrequently abuse them to their own destruction.

title: Nehemiah 9:27
text: Saviors; men raised up in providence to deliver them.

title: Nehemiah 9:28
text: Life often consists much in a contest between the goodness of God and the ingratitude and rebellion of men; and though, in answer to their cries, he often delivers them from their troubles, they as often forget his mercies and trample on his commands.

title: Nehemiah 9:33
text: Sin is the cause of all trouble; and God is holy, just, and good in all the judgments he brings upon those who commit it.

title: Nehemiah 9:36
text: We are servants; in bondage to the king of Persia.

title: Nehemiah 9:37
text: Dominion over our bodies; to employ them in wars and other services, at their pleasure.

title: Nehemiah 9:38
text: We make a sure covenant; a covenant, in all sincerity, with the Lord to obey him.

title: Nehemiah 10:1
text:
Those that sealed; that set their seal to the covenant mentioned at the close of the last chapter.  This list comprises only the chief men of the nation.  The rest of the people agreed to this covenant by oath,  Nehemiah 10:28-29 . 
 
All who know God should covenant to obey him, and having solemnly recognized their obligations to him should be careful to fulfil them. When this is done by ministers of the gospel and leading men among a people, multitudes will be ready to follow their example.

title: Nehemiah 10:29
text: They clave to their brethren; consented by an oath to the same covenant into which their chief men had entered to serve the Lord.  See note to  Nehemiah 10:1 .

title: Nehemiah 10:31
text: Abstinence from traffic and from all kinds of secular travelling and business on the Sabbath, is essential to a due observance of that holy day; and all who have covenanted to obey God, should remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy.

title: Nehemiah 10:32
text: While each individual should be disposed to bear his part in supporting the ministers, the worship, and the ordinances of the gospel, he should also give to habitual attendance upon them the influence of a conscientious and consistent example.

title: Nehemiah 10:37
text: Might have the tithes; rather, might give the tithes, and so in  Nehemiah 10:38 ; for the Levites gave to the priests a tithe of the tithes which they received from the people.  See  Nehemiah 12:47 .

title: Nehemiah 11:1
text:
One of ten to dwell in Jerusalem; Jerusalem at this time was only partially rebuilt, and was especially exposed to the attacks of the enemies of the Jews.  For the protection of the city, therefore, with its temple and temple services, it was necessary to require a certain portion of the people to reside there, who, if left to themselves, would have preferred some other place.  It is probable that, after takng the names of those who "willingly offered themselves,"  Nehemiah 11:2 , they cast lots for the remainder of this tenth part. 
 
It is a great blessing to dwell where spiritual privileges are enjoyed; and many will commend those that choose such places for their residence, who will not imitate their example.

title: Nehemiah 11:4
text: In selecting a place of residence, all should regard primarily the will of God, and seek a place in which they can most honor him, and secure the highest permanent benefit to themselves, their children, and their fellow men.

title: Nehemiah 11:16
text: The outward business of the house of God; providing the sacrifices, and making all needful preparation for the worship which the priests performed in the temple.

title: Nehemiah 11:20
text: Wherever people are called to live, the worship of God should be a part of their daily business; and in seeking first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, all needed blessings will be given them.

title: Nehemiah 11:24
text: Zerah--was at the king's hand; a commissioner or agent to transact his business with the people.

title: Nehemiah 12:1
text: That went up; from Babylon to Jerusalem.

title: Nehemiah 12:11
text:
vv 11,22. 
 
  Jaddua; commonly thought to be the high-priest who, according to Josephus, met Alexander the Great on his march to Jerusalem. 
 
  Darius the Persian; according to some, Darius Nothus; but the mention of him in connection with Jaddua has led many to think that Darius Codomanus, whom Alexander conquered, is meant.  It has been the opinion of many that this, and verse 11 above, are additions by a later hand after the death of Nehemiah.

title: Nehemiah 12:22
text:
See note to  Nehemiah 12:11 . 
 
When ministers of gospel are most faithful in the discharge of their appropriate duties, they take the best course, not only to honor God and advance the interests of true religion, but also to secure a comfortable support for themselves and their families.

title: Nehemiah 12:27
text: The dedication of the wall; as Jerusalem was designed to be a holy city, all parts of it were dedicated to the service of God.

title: Nehemiah 12:30
text: To be made instrumental in purifying others, ministers of the gospel must seek purification themselves, and endeavor in all things to set before the people a safe and useful example.

title: Nehemiah 12:31
text: Two great companies; one company went one way upon the wall with Ezra, and the other went the other way with Nehemiah.  They met on the opposite side of the city, and went together to the temple and offered their sacrifices of thanksgiving and praise, for having been enabled to finish the rebuilding and fortifying of the city.   Nehemiah 12:40-43

title: Nehemiah 12:40
text: Thanks should be rendered to God at the conclusion of every great and good work; and all the glory of success by all classes should be given to him.

title: Nehemiah 12:45
text:
Kept the ward of their God; discharged the duties assigned to them in God's service.  "Ward" is here used in the sense of a charge committed to one to keep. 
 
  The ward of the purification; the charge committed to them in respect to purification.  They were to see that nothing unclean entered the sanctuary. 
 
The influence of good men is felt long after they are dead; and each one should be careful to set an example which will be useful as long as it shall be remembered, and be instrumental when he is in heaven of preparing others for the same exceeding and eternal glory.

title: Nehemiah 13:1
text: The daily reading of a portion of Scripture is one of the most effectual means of communicating a knowledge of the will of God, and leading men to perform it.

title: Nehemiah 13:4
text:
Tobiah; the Ammonite, mentioned in  Nehemiah 2:10  and elsewhere as an enemy to the Jews. 
 
Alliance with the wicked is one of the cuases of increasing human corruption; and when ministers of religion are guilty of it, it tends to spread the evil through the community.

title: Nehemiah 13:5
text: A great chamber; in the courts of the temple, contrary to the command of God.

title: Nehemiah 13:6
text:
Was not I at Jerusalem; Nehemiah had left Judea and returned to Persia; and the above-mentioned abuses are supposed to have taken place during his absence. 
 
  Came I unto the king; the king of Persia, who reigned also over Babylon, and is here called the king of Babylon.  Nehemiah's return was twelve years after he first left Persia and went to Jerusalem. 
 
  Obtained I leave of the king; leave to go back again to Jerusalem. how long he now continued in Persia is not known, but from the account which he gives of the evil practices that had arisen during his absence,  Nehemiah 13:4 Nehemiah 13:5 Nehemiah 13:10 Nehemiah 13:15 , etc., it is probable that his absence was prolonged through several years. 
 
When the authority of pious magistrates is suspended, and those who rule encourage or connive at iniquity, it will be greatly increased; all who are disposed will then commit it with impunity and without restraint.

title: Nehemiah 13:8
text: Increase of iniquity greatly grieves the friends of God; and if they have the right and the ability, they will attempt speedily to restrain and remove it.  In this they may expect the aid of good men and the blessing of God.

title: Nehemiah 13:10
text:
Were fled; because they did not receive their support.  It is probable also that they were wanting in zeal for God's service. Compare  Malachi 1:10 . 
 
The withholding of adequate support from the ministers of the gospel, is one of the devices of Satan and his adherents to prevent a continuance of their labors.

title: Nehemiah 13:12
text: The tithe; a tenth part of their produce, for the support of the ministers of religion.

title: Nehemiah 13:15
text:
Treading wine-presses; to press the juice out of grapes, which was the usual manner of makng wine. 
 
The selling of food or other commodities, travelling for profit or pleasure, and the transaction of other secular business, on the Sabbath, are highly offensive to God; and tend to bring down upon individuals and the community his curse and wrath.

title: Nehemiah 13:19
text: As servile or secular labor on the Sabbath is inconsistent with the temporal welfare of the community, as well as the eternal good of individuals, it is the duty of the government by penal sanctions to prevent it, and if men will violate the law, to visit them with punishment; and when transgressors find the government and the people resolutely set against them, and that they cannot trample on the Sabbath with impunity, they will be likely to abstain from it.

title: Nehemiah 13:25
text: Plucked off their hair; a token of disgrace.

title: Nehemiah 13:26
text: Outlandish; heathen.

title: Nehemiah 13:28
text:
Sanballat the Horonite; governor of the Samaritans. 
 
Those who set at open defiance the laws of God and man, and whose continued presence is inconsistent with the welfare of the community, should not be permitted to live in it; and in all wise and good efforts to prevent their pestiferous influence, men may expect the aid of the enlightened, patriotic, and good, and the blessing of God.

title: Esther 1:4
text: Great power, wealth, and influence, tend to increase the pride of the human heart, and to lead men for the display of their own glory to scenes of festive and sensual indulgence, which expose them to vexation and sorrow in this world, and to endless woe in the world to come.

title: Esther 1:8
text: None did compel; none were compelled to drink, but each one drank, or refrained, as he pleased.

title: Esther 1:10
text: Wine is a mocker,and strong drink is raging.  When under its influence, reason is dethroned, and men often adopt measures disgraceful to themselves and ruinous to others.

title: Esther 1:12
text: Vashti refused to come; it was felt by her to be an indignity to be summoned thus into the presence of men, to gratify the caprice and vanity of the king; and this the king himself would have seen, had not his mind been clouded by the influence of wine.

title: Esther 1:13
text: Which knew the times; were acquainted with the history and customs of the kingdom.

title: Esther 1:15
text: Those who are clothed with authority should be careful not to give commands which cannot consistently be complied with, which can neither be obeyed nor disobeyed without involving others in distress and ruin.

title: Esther 1:16
text:
Done wrong--to all the people; by setting, as they alleged, a bad example. 
 
When men in high stations are surrounded by advisers who, instead of giving them faithful counsel, only flatter their vanity and consult their depraved passions, they will be led into unwise and unjust measures, by which great wrong will be done to those under their power.

title: Esther 1:19
text:
That it be not altered; it was then the established usage, that laws of the Medes and Persians, once passed, could not be altered.  No law of divorce such as this has any divine sanction. 
 
As human laws are more of less imperfect, adn are at times palpably unjust, the idea that they are never to be altered is the offspring of self-sufficiency and pride.

title: Esther 2:1
text: What is done in a passion is often a source of deep regret; and if men do not change their conduct, but continue in sin and folly, choosing rather to do this than to acknowledge their error, they must in the end by miserable, eat the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices.

title: Esther 2:4
text: Sin in prospect appears to those who love it very different from what it does after it has been committed.  It promises good; but at last, bites like a serpent and stings like an adder.

title: Esther 2:7
text:
Hadassah; her Hebrew name, signifying, Myrtle. 
 
  Esther; the Persian name given her upon her advancement to the dignity of queen.  It signifies, Star. 
 
Kindness to orphans is well-pleasing to God, and he often follows it with special manifestatons of his favor.

title: Esther 2:10
text: Ability and disposition to keep secret what should not be published, is a valuable trait of character, and should be cultivated by all who are intrusted with great and important concerns.

title: Esther 2:16
text:
In the seventh year of his reign; about four years after the divorce of Vashti,  Esther 1:3 . 
 
God is able to overrule those actions of men that are in themselves neither wise nor righteous, for the accomplishment of his own most wise and righteous counsels.  Thus the divorce Vashti prepared the way for the elevation of Esther to the royal dignity, with all its important consequences to the Jewish people.

title: Esther 2:17
text: When God sees best, he can give his people favor even with those who rebel against him; and all the influence he gives to any should be employed to promote his glory and the good of men.

title: Esther 2:18
text: A release; a remission of tribute.

title: Esther 2:19
text:
Were gathered together the second time; the meaning of these words is not certain; they may refer to a second gathering of fair virgins from whom concubines for the king were to be selected, after that first gathering for the choice of a queen. 
 
  Sat in the king's gate; these words imply that he had received an office in the king's palace, and sat in his gate, according to the custom at the Persian court, ready to discharge whatever duties might be required of him.

title: Esther 2:21
text:
Sought to lay hand on the king; conspired against his life. 
 
While the wicked are devising wicked devices and seeking the ruin of others, God may be preparing to overrule it for their own destruction, and for the salvation of his people.

title: Esther 2:23
text: The book of the chronicles; the register of the affairs of the kingdom, kept in the royal palace.   Esther 1:1-10:3 Esther 6:1

title: Esther 3:1
text:
Haman; supposed to have been an Amalekite, and a descendant of one of their ancient kings.   Exodus 17:14 Deuteronomy 25:17-19  
 
Despots not unfrequently advance to places of honor and power the most wicked of their subjects.

title: Esther 3:2
text: Bowed not; it was not contrary to the laws and usages of the Jews that they should render to rulers the customary marks of honor, even to prostration on the earth, where these would not be misunderstood.  But Mordecai seem to have felt that he could not, in the present circumstances, render homage to this vile favorite of the king, without degrading his character and his religion before the eyes of the heathen.

title: Esther 3:3
text: When rulers require their subjects to disobey God, it is the duty of subjects to disobey them; and though this may expose them to the wrath of men, it will meet the approbation of God.

title: Esther 3:4
text: He had told them that he was a Jew; he seems to have excused himself from bowing before Haman on the ground of his religion as a Jew.

title: Esther 3:6
text: A man may be so wicked as to regard his own glory more than he does the lives of his fellow men.

title: Esther 3:7
text:
Cast Pur--the lot; to determine the time when the Jews should be destroyed.  This was done in accordance with the heathenish idea that one day is more lucky than another for the accomplishment of an undertaking. 
 
The lot may be cast into the lap, but the disposal will be of God; and he may so order it as to prevent the end it was intended to subserve.

title: Esther 3:8
text: To suffer them; suffer them to live.

title: Esther 3:9
text: The charge of the business; not the business of destroying the Jews, but the pecuniary matters of the king.  Haman offers to pay to the managers of the king's treasury this sum, if the king will grant the decree; intending, no doubt, to collect it out of the spoils of the Jews.  Compare  Esther 4:7 .

title: Esther 3:10
text: Took his ring--and gave it unto Haman; his signet-ring.  Thus he gave him authority to accomplish his wishes.

title: Esther 3:11
text:
The silver is given to thee; by these words the king releases Haman from the condition proposed by him,  Esther 3:9 . 
 
For the gratification of a worthless favorite, a monarch will sometimes sacrifice the happiness, and even the lives of thousands of his subjects.

title: Esther 3:15
text:
Shushan was perplexed; on account of the decree to destroy the Jews. 
 
The triumph of the wicked is short; and while Providence for a time seem to favor them, and they glory in their expected success, they may be working out their own destruction.

title: Esther 4:2
text: Came even before the king's gate; according to the usages of those times and countries, Mordecai could have no direct access to the queen. He therefore took this method of making known to Esther the calamity that had befallen him and his nation.

title: Esther 4:3
text:
Great mourning--and fasting, and weeping; they humbled themselves deeply before God.   Esther 9:31 Jonah 3:8-9  
 
This is a state of trial, and great calamities may come upon us when we least expect them.  Our interest and duty both require that we should so live as to be prepared at all times to meet such events; and when they come, instead of sinking in despair, we should look to God for help.

title: Esther 4:5
text: Diligent inquiry into the sufferings of others for the purpose of relieving them, well becomes those who are at ease; as they know not how soon they also may need sympathy and assistance.

title: Esther 4:8
text: It is proper to make application to men, if they have the power to help us; but while so doing, we should also make supplication to God, that he would incline men to use their power in such a manner as to afford needed relief.

title: Esther 4:14
text:
Then shall--enlargement--arise to the Jews from another place; by this Mordecai showed his confidence in God, and his expectation that He would in some way grant them deliverance. 
 
Strong confidence in God, and expectation that he will in his own time and way appear for those who put their trust in him, is a preparation to experience his salvation.

title: Esther 4:16
text:
I also and my maidens will fast; this fast of Esther and her people was doubtless attended with earnest supplications that the Most High would interfere in their behalf. 
 
Show good men the path of duty, and though it be at the hazard of all earthly things, even of life itself, they will walk in it, committing themselves and all their interests, mortal and immortal, to Him who ruleth over all ans who doeth all things.

title: Esther 5:3
text: God often favors his people, not only equal to, but beyond their expectations; doing for them exceeding abundantly above all that they ask or think; and the surest way of obtaining the favor of men, is first to secure the favor of God.

title: Esther 5:6
text: Although men are prone to change, and but little dependence can be placed upon their promises, God can keep them of one mind as long as the good of his people requires.   Esther 7:2

title: Esther 5:8
text: Though delays are often dangerous, yet sometimes they are essential to success; and wisdom from above is needful in order to judge rightly as to the time as well as the manner of attempting to execute difficult and important designs.

title: Esther 5:11
text: No favors of mere creatures can satisfy the wants of the soul, or keep it from being wretched while seeking supremely its own glory, regardless of the glory of God and the good of mankind.

title: Esther 5:13
text: All this availeth me nothing; it did nothing towards makng him happy, or satisfying the wants of his soul.

title: Esther 5:14
text:
Fifty cubits high; about seventy-five feet. 
 
  Go thou in merrily; being relieved from thy trouble by the death of Mordecai. 
 
The measures which men take for the destruction of others often prove the means of their own; and while they glory in anticipated victory, they sink into irretrievable ruin.

title: Esther 6:1
text:
That night could not the king sleep; God so ordered it, to make him acquainted with what Mordecai had done. 
 
  The chronicles; the records of the kingdom. 
 
Sleep is a blessing which comes from God; and when permitted quietly and safely to enjoy it, we should recognize his goodness and render him thanks for his mercy; and if kept awake during the night, we should so occupy our minds as to honor God, and advance our growth in grace and our highest usefulness.

title: Esther 6:3
text: Ingratitude is a common sin, and we may perform for others the most important services and yet receive from them no reward.  But actions performed for God will never be forgotten; even the giving of a cup of cold water for his sake to one of his disciples will be acknowledged and graciously rewarded before the assembled world.

title: Esther 6:4
text: The design of God in leading a man from one place to another, may be very different from his own in going.  While his heart deviseth its way, the Lord directeth his steps; and though there be many devices in a man's heart, the counsel of the Lord that shall stand.

title: Esther 6:6
text: When a man delights to honor himself supremely, he thinks that others should do the same; and if they do not he is often ready to overwhelm them in ruin.

title: Esther 6:12
text: Having his head covered; a token of mortification, chagrin, and disappointment.

title: Esther 6:13
text:
Be of the seed of the Jews--shalt surely fall before him; the more sagacious among the heathen had some general knowledge of the wonderful dealings of Jehovah, "the God of heaven," towards his covenant people; and they had noticed the efficacy of his favor towards those who were his faithful worshippers: perhaps, also, they were acquainted with the history of Daniel and his companions.  From all this, as well as from their knowledge of the suddenness with which the king transferred his affections from one favorite to another, they surely gathered the approaching fall of Haman. 
 
God in his providence taketh the wise in their own craftiness, the counsel of the froward he carrieth headlong; and he may so evidently work against a man, that even worldly sagacity may foresee his downfall and ruin.

title: Esther 7:4
text:
The king's damage; by making so large a number of his subjects slaves. 
 
Persecution is always detrimental to rulers and subjects.

title: Esther 7:6
text: When the doings of the wicked are brought to light, they see that they have reason to fear; and that nothing but mercy can save them from ruin.  The fear of the wicked cometh upon him.  He is taken in his own net, and entangled in his own devices.

title: Esther 7:8
text: They covered Haman's face; a token that he was condemned by the king.

title: Esther 7:9
text: When men begin to fall, many who have before favored them turn against them and unite to hasten their ruin.

title: Esther 8:2
text:
The king took off his ring--and gave it unto Mordecai; his signet-ring.  Thus he invested him with full authority. 
 
Men cannot tell what will become of their riches and honors after they are dead.  The wealth of the wicked is often laid up for the just; and when the good of his church requires, God can cause the one to give place to the other.

title: Esther 8:3
text: The mischief which men do while they live, often endures long after they are dead; and were it not for the overruling providence of God, would continue to the end of time.

title: Esther 8:6
text: The exposure of our relatives and friends to destruction is peculiarly distressing; and should lead us earnestly to seek and fervently to pray for their salvation.

title: Esther 8:10
text: With the utmost practicable haste, the way of salvation should be made known to all people, and they be urged to embrace it and live.

title: Esther 8:11
text: To stand for their life; in self-defence, and to destroy those who should attempt to destroy them.  The first decree for the destruction of the Jews was not formally repealed, since edicts sealed with the king's seal were unchangeable; but a new decree was made, empowering the Jews to defend themselves and destroy their enemies.

title: Esther 8:15
text:
In royal apparel; in token of his being clothed, as prime-minster, with royal authority. 
 
Sudden changes await the people of God; and as sudden await those who oppose them, or neglect the great salvation.  Lazarus may one day lie at the rich man's gate full of sores, and the next day be in glory; while the rich man, who is one day clothed in purple and fine linen, may the next be in torment.  The hope of the wicked shall perish; while light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart.

title: Esther 9:1
text: The triumph of the wicked is short, and their most confident expectations will come to naught.   Proverbs 11:7

title: Esther 9:3
text: Many are more influenced by the fear of man than by the fear of God; and when rulers are on the side of right, many will externally follow their example.

title: Esther 9:10
text: The wickedness of parents may prove the occasion of destruction to their children; and efforts to destroy the church of God may ruin not only those who make them, but all who are induced to follow their example.   Esther 9:25 Esther 3:6

title: Esther 9:13
text: The gallows; the one, it is supposed, which Haman had prepared for Mordecai, and on which he was himself hanged.

title: Esther 9:16
text: One man, by his wickedness, may be instrumental in the destruction of thousands.   Exodus 7:1-14:31

title: Esther 9:19
text:
With the people of God, darkness may endure for a night, but light cometh in the morning. 
 
"Let those that sow in sadness wait Till the fair harvest come; They shall confess their sheaves are great, And shout the blessings home."

title: Esther 9:21
text: Fourteenth day of the month of Adar; this month answered to part of February and March.  The feast of Purim, or the lot, thus instituted, is observed by the Jews to this day.

title: Esther 9:28
text: Special mercies demand special thanksgivings to the Author and Finisher of all good, and call us to imitate the Saviour's example in doing good as we have opportunity and ability, to those who may need and feel our influence.

title: Esther 9:29
text: This second letter of Purim; the first letter mentioned,  Esther 9:20 , seems to have been more of the nature of a recommendation, but the second letter was authoritative.

title: Esther 9:30
text: With words of peace and truth; kind words of truth according to the will of God.

title: Esther 9:31
text:
The fastings; to keep in mind those observed by Esther and the Jews.   Esther 4:16-17  
 
  Their cry; for deliverance from the machinations of their enemies.

title: Esther 9:32
text: In the book; the records of the acts that were passed on this occasion.

title: Esther 10:1
text:
A tribute; a tax to be paid into the king's treasury. 
 
As civil government is an ordinance of God is not mentioned, yet we here see most illustrious and striking displays of his character and government: that he ruleth over all; maketh the wrath of man to praise him and restraineth the remainder thereof; that the greatest and the smallest events are under his control, and are all so directed by him as to promote the salvation of his people and the destruction of their and his enemies.

title: Esther 10:2
text:
The book of the chronicles; the book that contained the records of the kingdoms of Media and Persia. 
 
Records of the acts of governments should be fairly and faithfully kept, for the benefit of the present and future generations.

title: Esther 10:3
text:
The names of rulers who are acceptable to the people, who seek their peace and prosperity, and who adopt such measures as are best suited to promote them, will be handed down with honor to posterity.  They are special gifts of God, and should call forth devout gratitude to him from all who enjoy the benefits of their administration. 
 
Although in the book of Esther the name of God is not mentioned, yet we here see most illustrious and striking displays of his character and government: that he ruleth over all; maketh the wrath of man to praise him and restraineth the remainder thereof; that the greatest and the smallest events are under his control, and are all so directed by him as to promote the salvation of his people and the destruction of their and his enemies.

title: Job 1:1
text:
Uz; a district in Arabia, east of Palestine. 
 
  Perfect and upright; a man who habitually feared God and obeyed all his commandments.  Like Zachariah and Elizabeth, he was "righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless."  Luke 1:6  
 
  Feared God; with childlike, reverential, holy fear. 
 
  Eschewed; departed from, avoided. 
 
God sometimes bestows on his children great wealth, numerous friends, and abundance of earthly blessings, and thus increases their obligations to love and serve him.

title: Job 1:4
text:
His day; his birthday,  Job 3:1-3 . 
 
It is proper to partake of the bounties of Providence with gratitude and joy; and pleasant when brothers and sisters love one another, rejoice in each other's society, and together celebrate the goodness of God.

title: Job 1:5
text:
Sent and sanctified them; he directed them to perform those outward cleansings which were a sign of that purity of heart and life which God requires of all his worshippers, and Job inculcated on his children by both precept and example. 
 
  Cursed God in their hearts; dishonored him by unworthy and wicked thoughts of him. 
 
  Thus did Job continually; habitually, after each yearly feast of his assembled households. 
 
Seasons of feasting are seasons of peculiar danger.  While men partake freely of God's gifts they are tempted to forget or in some other way to dishonor the giver, and thus they need his pardoning mercy through Jesus Christ.

title: Job 1:6
text: The sons of God; the angelic hosts, as in  Job 38:7 .  The scene of this transaction is laid in heaven.  Compare  I Kings 22:19 .

title: Job 1:9
text:
For naught; without being paid for it.  Satan means to insinuate that Job's piety is wholly selfish, and will vanish as soon as he finds that it ceases to bring to him a reward of earthly good. 
 
Those who contend that all religion is selfish, and that good men serve God only because he does them good, resemble Satan and take part with him in promoting his cause.

title: Job 1:10
text:
Made a hedge about him; to defend him from all evil. 
 
  Blessed the work of his hands; rewarded him abundantly for his seeming piety.

title: Job 1:11
text:
Touch all that he hath; destroy it. 
 
  Curse thee to thy face; openly, with daring impiety.

title: Job 1:12
text:
Upon himself put not forth thy hand; do not injure him in his person. 
 
Satan, if permitted by God, may not only tempt men to sin, but bring upon them great and sore calamities.

title: Job 1:15
text: Sabeans; an Arab tribe.

title: Job 1:17
text: The Chaldeans; a troop of pillagers from near the Euphrates.

title: Job 1:20
text:
Rent his mantle, and shaved his head; in token of deep mourning. 
 
Good men will not overlook God's hand when calamities come upon them, nor fail to humble themselves before him.

title: Job 1:21
text:
Shall I return thither; to the womb of the earth, which is the mother of all mankind.  He uses the word "womb" in a twofold sense, first literally, and then figuratively. 
 
Nothing so sustains the soul in the day of severe trial, as the thought that God sends it.

title: Job 1:22
text: Charged God foolishly; that is, attributed folly to God.

title: Job 2:3
text:
He holdeth fast his integrity; persevered in yielding obedience to God, notwithstanding his calamities. 
 
Though true religion has been proved a thousand times to be genuine, yet Satan and his agents still insist that it is all hypocrisy and selfishness.  To show the falsehood of this, God sometimes suffers him to visit his people with calamities, while he so sustains them by his grace as to silence the objections of foolish men.

title: Job 2:4
text: Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life; Satan here renews his charge of selfishness against Job.  True he has lost his property and his children, but his person yet remains unharmed.  Should God touch him here, he will renounce his allegiance to God, and blaspheme his name.  To show the falsehood of this, exhibit the nature of true religion, and prepare Job for greater good in the end, God permitted Satan to try it.

title: Job 2:7
text: With sore boils; his disease is generally regarded to have been a malignant and painful species of leprosy.

title: Job 2:8
text: Potsherd; a piece of earthen ware.

title: Job 2:9
text: Our most intimate friends may become our greatest tempters, and thus, unless resisted, our most dangerous foes.

title: Job 2:10
text:
Shall we not receive evil? though Satan was the instrument, yet Job viewed his trials as coming from God; and as such, he humbly submitted to them. 
 
God is wise and good, not only in the mercies which he bestows, but in the trials which he sends or permits.  While grateful for the one, we should be submissive under the other, and thus strive to honor him in both.

title: Job 2:12
text:
Knew him not; he was so altered by his disease, that at first they did not recognize him. 
 
  They lifted up their voice and wept; when they saw how dreadfully he was afflicted. 
 
Sickness and trials may so emaciate and disfigure our bodies that our friends will hardly know us, and our sufferings be such that they can give us no relief.

title: Job 3:1
text: His day; the day of his birth, feeling that he had been deprived of all his possessions and of all capacity to enjoy life, and that thus existence had become a heavy calamity to him.  The language of Job throughout this chapter is that of passionate complaint against God's providence, and in using it he sinned; but Satan could not prevail with him to curse his Maker.

title: Job 3:3
text: A good man under trials may become fretful and peevish, have hard thoughts of God and his ways, and may say things which he will afterwards see to be foolish and wicked, and of which he will be utterly ashamed.   Job 42:3-6

title: Job 3:8
text:
Them--that curse the day; magicians, who were supposed to have power to curse certain days, as well as persons.  Compare what Balak says to Balaam,  Numbers 22:6 . 
 
  To raise up their mourning; or, to raise up leviathan.  He would have the most powerful enchanters employed, who, according to the superstitious belief of the multitude, were able to raise up leviathan from the deep.

title: Job 3:11
text: Men if left to themselves under trials, may wish that they were dead, and be tempted sometimes even to kill themselves; but this is rebellion against God, and is the way to increase their own sorrows.  I Samuel 28:15-20 I Samuel 31:4 Matthew 27:3-5 Mark 14:21

title: Job 3:12
text: Prevent me; in the old English sense of anticipating, being ready beforehand to meet one.

title: Job 3:14
text: Desolate places for themselves; cities in the desert; or perhaps sepulchres, which they built where they might rest and be quiet.  Had he died at his birth, Job thought he should have rested with equal quietness.

title: Job 3:19
text: There; in the grave, which Job here regards as a place of rest from the sufferings of life.

title: Job 3:20
text: Unto the bitter in soul; to him who pines in misery.

title: Job 3:21
text: Dig for it; earnestly desire and seek it.

title: Job 3:23
text:
Whose way is hid; so that he can see no possibility of escape from his sufferings. 
 
  Hedged in; so that he is shut up to calamity, without the hope of release. 
 
Men sometimes wonder why it is that God preserves their lives, when they seem to be receiving no good themselves, and doing no good to others.  But God has wise and good reasons; and through their preservation and trials, may bless not only them, but multitudes of others to the end of time and to eternity.   Romans 14:7 I Timothy 1:16

title: Job 3:25
text: The thing which I greatly feared is come upon me; or, "When I fear a fear, it comes upon me:" calamities more and more dreadful follow each other in quick succession.

title: Job 4:3
text:
The weak hands; persons that were ready to faint and despond under trouble. 
 
The ability and disposition to give instruction to the ignorant, consolation to the sorrowful, and encouragement to the despairing, are valuable traits of character, which should be diligently cultivated and faithfully improved for the benefit of men.

title: Job 4:5
text:
It; distress. 
 
It is much easier to preach than to practise; and those instructions which we give to others, and which sometimes comfort and support them, we at other times fail properly to apply for our own direction and benefit.

title: Job 4:6
text: Is not this thy fear; that is, thy religious fear, or thy piety. The meaning of Elihu, according to our version, is, that Job's fear of God, trust in him, and uprightness of life, for which he has enjoyed so high a reputation, ought now, if they be indeed genuine, to sustain him; since it is not possible, under the righteous government of God, that the innocent and righteous should perish.  But many propose to render, "Should not thy fear be thy confidence? thy hope, should it not even be the righteousness of thy ways?" which, however, comes to substantially the same idea.

title: Job 4:7
text:
Who ever perished, being innocent? this is true if we look to the final end of righteous, but not true of we look simply to their outward lot in this world; and here lay the mistake of Job's friends.  They looked upon this world as a state not merely of trial, but of retribution.  In this Job justly differed from them; and this was the point of controversy between them. 
 
The idea of Eliphaz and his friends, that good men will not be afflicted or suffer a violent death, and that of course the afflictions of Job proved him to be what Satan accused him of being, a hypocrite, was false.  By adopting this idea and applying it to Job, they joined themselves with Satan in tormenting him.   John 16:33 Revelation of John 7:14

title: Job 4:8
text:
Plough--sow; practise. 
 
  Reap the same; experience the fruit or effects of their sins.  Job 4:9-11

title: Job 4:10
text: The roaring of the lion; the lion here represents haughty and powerful sinners, who prosper for a while, and then are violently destroyed.  Compare  Psalms 37:35-36 .

title: Job 4:12
text: Secretly brought; revealed in a dream or vision.

title: Job 4:13
text: Dreams are not now to be relied on; and yet, if they are the means of suggesting important thoughts and leading to useful reflections, they should be gratefully acknowledged and made subservient to our own good and that of others.

title: Job 4:16
text: It; the spirit.

title: Job 4:17
text: More just than God? so that he can rightly arraign the conduct of his Maker? Ought he not rather to submit to all His dispensations?

title: Job 4:18
text: In comparison with God, all created wisdom, power, or goodness are as nothing.  His perfections infinitely surpass all finite conceptions.

title: Job 4:19
text: Them that dwell in houses of clay; a figurative description of man's mortal frame, as weak and perishable.

title: Job 4:20
text: From morning to evening; either within the space of a single day, as a poetic description of the brevity of life; or, all day long, that is, continually.

title: Job 5:1
text:
Answer thee; as a friend and patron, ready to support thy cause. 
 
  The saints; here probably the holy angels. 
 
Men sometimes think that all the good agree in opinion with themselves, and that those who do not are wicked.

title: Job 5:2
text: Envy; more exactly, indignation.  It is the wrath and indignation of one who rebels against the discipline of God's providence, which Eliphaz means.  These are the means of ruin to the wicked who indulge them.

title: Job 5:3
text:
Foolish; here, as throughout the book of Job, the foolish are the wicked, who are destitute of true wisdom. 
 
  Suddenly I cursed his habitation; I saw destruction suddenly come upon his habitation, and pronounced it accursed. 
 
It needs no spirit of prophecy to foretell the ruin of such as continue in a course of disobedience to God.

title: Job 5:4
text: Crushed in the gate; condemned in the place where judgments were issued.

title: Job 5:5
text: Even out of the thorns; here probably a hedge of thorns intended for the protection of the harvest.

title: Job 5:6
text:
Cometh not forth of the dust; affliction does not come by chance; it is ordered by God, and therefore should be cheerfully submitted to. 
 
As troubles do not come by chance, but are directed by infinite wisdom and goodness, for most benevolent ends, they should be borne with patience, and cheerful submission to the perfect will of God.

title: Job 5:7
text: As the sparks fly upward; it is as natural for fallen man to sin and suffer, as for sparks to fly upward.

title: Job 5:8
text: I would seek unto God; if I were in thy place; thus expressing the duty of all men in affliction.

title: Job 5:12
text: No wisdom but that which comes from above will guide a man in the path of truth and duty, or ultimately meet with success.

title: Job 5:13
text:
The wise; the worldly wise. 
 
  The froward; the perverse who disobey God.

title: Job 5:15
text: The poor; the afflicted, who trust in God.

title: Job 5:17
text:
Whom God correcteth; and who receives correction in a proper manner. 
 
Trust in God and supreme devotion to him, will sanctify every trial while it lasts, and in due time secure certain, full, and eternal deliverance.

title: Job 5:19
text: In six troubles--in seven; a definite is here put for a large indefinite number.

title: Job 5:21
text: Hid; safe, where the scourge of the tongue cannot find thee.  "The scourge of the tongue" represents those false accusations which expose a man to the spoiling of his goods, to imprisonment, and even death.

title: Job 5:23
text: In league with the stones; they shall not hurt thee.

title: Job 5:24
text: Not sin; not wander, err, or miss the way to his house, but find it safe as he left it.

title: Job 5:25
text: Great; numerous and prosperous.

title: Job 5:26
text: In a full age; not meet a premature death.

title: Job 5:27
text:
We have searched it; learned from observation, that those who feel and act right, are delivered or saved from trouble; and those only continue to be afflicted, who continue to feel and act wrong.  From this Eliphaz would draw the erroneous conclusion, that the continuance of Job's afflictions proved him to be as Satan affirmed, a hypocrite, or a very selfish, wicked man. 
 
Human reason and observation, without revelation, are unsafe guides; and none, unless enlightened by God, will have such views of his character and ways as lead to safety and success.

title: Job 6:3
text:
Heavier than the sand; very great, insupportable. 
 
  Are swallowed up; are insufficient to express my calamity. 
 
Complaints under calamities, instead of lessening, generally increase them, and unfit the mind to bear them with patience, or receive the benefit they might otherwise occasion.

title: Job 6:4
text: Arrows of the Almighty; such distresses as God alone can inflict.

title: Job 6:5
text: Loweth the ox over his fodder? the beast does not complain without reason; nor, as Job contended, did he.

title: Job 6:6
text: Unsavory be eaten without salt? or, unsavory for want of salt, be eaten?  his calamities are to him as unsavory food, causing bitter complaint.

title: Job 6:7
text: Trials from which we instinctively shrink in prosperity, sometimes become so wearisome in adversity, that we wish for death.

title: Job 6:8
text: The thing that I long for; immediate death.

title: Job 6:10
text:
Harden myself in sorrow; or, exult in sorrow; that is, in the present connection, in the pangs of death. 
 
  Not spare; to cut short my life. 
 
  Not concealed the words of the Holy One; not denied his commands, but made them the rule of my life.

title: Job 6:11
text:
Should hope; for returning health and prosperity. 
 
  What is mine end; what favorable issue to my present calamities can I look for?

title: Job 6:13
text: Is not my help in me--wisdom driven quite from me? or, as we may render, "Is it not so that I have no help in me, and counsel is driven quite from me?"

title: Job 6:14
text:
He forsaketh; he who does not show pity to the afflicted, sins against the Almighty. 
 
The distresses of others should draw forth our compassion and kindness; and the manifestaton of a contrary spirit, is a sin not only against men, but against God.

title: Job 6:15
text: As a brook; a brook that abounds with water for a time, and then dries away.

title: Job 6:16
text: The ice; that melted from the mountains.

title: Job 6:19
text: Tema--Sheba; countries of Arabia.

title: Job 6:20
text: Hoped; to find water in the channel of the river in the desert.

title: Job 6:21
text:
Ye are nothing; of no worth to me as comforters, like the brooks that pass away. 
 
Expectations of help from earthly friends are often disappointed; but those which are placed on God will in the end be more than realized.

title: Job 6:22
text: Did I say, Bring unto me? did he request his friends to help him? All that he had asked of them was comforting words.  But these were denied him.

title: Job 6:25
text: Right words; words of truth, which, as Job contended, the words of Eliphaz were not.

title: Job 6:27
text: Overwhelm the fatherless; or, cast lots upon the fatherless; that is, upon his substance, after spoiling him.  He means to say, You exhibit towards me a similar cruelty; for I am in the condition of a fatherless child overwhelmed with sorrow, and without helpers.

title: Job 6:29
text: Return, I pray you; and address him in a different manner, one that should not impute to him iniquity, but should admit that he was upright and sincere.

title: Job 6:30
text: Discern; between good and evil in himself.

title: Job 7:1
text:
An appointed time; or, a warfare. 
 
  He means that his whole life is, as it were, a warfare. 
 
  Like the days of a hireling; occupied with hard labor, so that he longs for their close,  Job 7:2  
 
The length of human life is fixed by God; and all the days of our appointed time we should wait with patience, and labor with diligence, till our change come.

title: Job 7:2
text: The shadow; of evening.

title: Job 7:3
text: Months of vanity--wearisome nights; so that, like the hireling, I long to have the day of life close.

title: Job 7:5
text: No perfection of human character will exempt men in this world from trials; and none but those who have experienced them, can realize the difficulty of exercising at all times a calm, quiet, peaceful submission under them.

title: Job 7:6
text: Without hope; of recovery, or any relief except in death.

title: Job 7:8
text: Are upon me--am not; or, "shall be upon me, and I shall not be." Thou shalt seek me, but I shall no more be found in the land of the living,  Job 7:21 .

title: Job 7:12
text: Thou settest a watch over me; guardest me as if I needed strong restraint.

title: Job 7:13
text: Quiet and refreshing rest in sleep is the gift of God, and a blessing the greatness of which no one who has not for a time been deprived of it will duly appreciate.

title: Job 7:16
text: Let me alone; cease from troubling me during the brief day of life.

title: Job 7:17
text: Magnify him; make so much account of him in the way of chastisement and discipline.

title: Job 7:19
text: Till I swallow down my spittle; a proverbial expression, meaning, till I have a little respite.

title: Job 7:20
text:
Set me as a mark; for the arrows of the Almighty. 
 
All men have sinned, and deserve all that they suffer; and the only sure way of deliverance is in acknowledging their transgressions, and looking up to Him who is exalted to give repentance, that he would freely and abundantly pardon.

title: Job 7:21
text: For now shall I sleep in the dust; he means, that if God does not soon pardon his transgression, and restore to him the light of his countenance, there will be no more opportunity to show him kindness, since he is passing down rapidly to the grave.

title: Job 8:3
text:
Doth God pervert judgment? Job had not asserted this, though Bildad speaks as if he had. 
 
It is common for men in controversy to impute sentiments to their opponents which they do not hold, and to charge them with consequences which they reject and abhor.

title: Job 8:6
text:
He would awake for thee; God would remove his calamities and make him prosperous; and because he did not do it, Bildad like Eliphaz erroneously concluded that Job was a wicked man.  Their error was, in supposing that the outward condition of men in this world was according to their character. 
 
Many errors arise from confounding this state of trial with the future state of retribution.  God will arise for the deliverance and salvation of his people, but it may not be in this world.  Here they may have tribulation, but in heaven they will have rest.   I Corinthians 15:19

title: Job 8:8
text:
Prepare thyself; meaning, Direct thy attention. 
 
  The search of their fathers; the maxims concerning God's dealings with men which their fathers have searched out; those, namely, contained in  Job 8:11-19 . 
 
Much may be learned from the experience and observation of those who have gone before us; but their principles as well as our own should be tried by the unerring word of God, and if not in accordance with that should be rejected.

title: Job 8:9
text: We are but of yesterday; our life is too short to enable us to reach the wisdom of the fathers, who lived much longer than we, and had more time for observation.

title: Job 8:10
text: They; the fathers.

title: Job 8:11
text: Can the flag grow without water? as the flag withers as soon as the ground becomes dry, so is the prosperity of hypocrites short-lived.

title: Job 8:13
text: That on which hypocrites depend will, at death, if not before, utterly fail them.

title: Job 8:15
text: It shall not stand; that on which he depends shall give way and disappoint him.

title: Job 8:16
text: He is green before the sun; the hypocrite flourishes a while, like a luxuriant plant.

title: Job 8:17
text:
Are wrapped about the heap; about the heap of stones.  This figure has been interpreted in different ways; but, from its connection, it seems to denote the vigorous growth of the plant. 
 
  Seeth the place of stones; the place of stones is the same as the heap just mentioned.  This he sees by reaching it with his roots.

title: Job 8:18
text:
If he destroy him; if one destroy him; or, if God destroy him; that is, the hypocrite under the figure of a plant. 
 
  From his place; where he is growing so luxuriantly.  It is a sudden destruction which Bildad means to set forth.  Compare  Job 5:3 . 
 
  It shall deny him; the place where he was lately growing shall deny all knowledge of him.  The above all goes upon the erroneous supposition that men are always treated in this world according to their character.

title: Job 8:19
text:
This is the joy of his way; this is its sudden end. 
 
  Shall others grow; other plants in his stead; that is, good men shall succeed to his prosperity.

title: Job 8:20
text: Though God will not cast away the righteous, or help the wicked in the future world, yet in this, the wicked may be in great prosperity, and the righteous in great adversity.   Psalms 73:1 Psalms 73:15

title: Job 9:1
text: That we may understand the true attitude of Job in this painful controversy with his friends, the present chapter should be carefully studied, as furnishing the key to his discourses throughout.  While he indignantly repels the charge of being an ungodly man and a hypocrite, he does not deny his general sinfulness before his Maker.  Should God call him, or any other man, into judgment, he could not answer Him for one of a thousand,  Job 9:3 .  God is every way infinite.  As none can withstand his almighty power, so none can call him to account for his dealings.  If Job should attempt to contend with him, his divine majesty would utterly overwhelm him.  All his arguments to maintain his innocence would be turned against him,   Job 9:20 Job 9:30 Job 9:31 .  He knows that God is righteous, yet he is conscious to himself of having lived an upright life.  His calamity is to him an inexplicable mystery.  All he can say of it is, that God  "destroyeth the perfect and the wicked,"  Job 9:22-24 .  The thought of God's repeated and terrible blows overwhelms him, and fills him with despair.  It is his Maker's determination to hold him guilty; why should he waste time and strength in justifying himself?   Job 9:27-31   Yet if God would lay aside his chastising rod and his terrible majesty, and permit him to converse with him, as a man with a man, then he would plead his cause before him with confidence, being sustained by the consciousness of his uprightness,  Job 9:32-35 .

title: Job 9:2
text: I know it is so; that man in his best estate is a sinner, and that God in all his dealings is just.

title: Job 9:3
text:
Answer him; excuse or justify himself, in one of a thousand of his actions. 
 
The justice of God in all his dispensations should be taken for granted; and whatever may be a man's views of himself, his only safety is in the mercy and grace of God.

title: Job 9:5
text: They know not; he does it suddenly, unexpectedly.

title: Job 9:6
text: Which shaketh the earth; as an earthquake.

title: Job 9:10
text: As the greatness of God is past finding our, so the reason of many of his dealings is to creatures unknown, and can be revealed only by himself.

title: Job 9:13
text: The proud helpers; who are banded together to support each other in a wicked cause.

title: Job 9:15
text:
Though I were righteous; not conscious of sin. 
 
  I would make supplication; sensible that God might see sins where he did not.

title: Job 9:16
text:
Had called; had called God to argue my cause with him. 
 
  That he had hearkened; that he would so listen to my words that they should be of any account with him. 
 
Unbelief shuts out God from the soul, and prevents it from rejoicing in or seeing the manifestations of his mercy.

title: Job 9:17
text: Multilpieth my wounds without cause; the cause of which Job could not see.

title: Job 9:18
text: To take my breath; his trials were constant as well as great.

title: Job 9:20
text: All efforts at self-justification in the sight of God, are proofs of a want of submission to him, and only increase the difficulties they are intended to remove.

title: Job 9:21
text:
Though I were perfect; in his own estimation; yet he did not know the state of his own soul, as God did. 
 
  I would despise my life; submit to any trials that God might lay upon him.

title: Job 9:22
text:
This is one thing; God has one rule for the righteous and the wicked: he sends calamities on both.  In this opinion Job differed entirely from his three friends. 
 
Since this world is one of trial, and not of strict retribution, we must not be surprised or discouraged if things happen outwardly in many respects alike to the righteous and the wicked; remembering that in the end God will cause all to see the difference between him that fears, and him that despises his Maker.

title: Job 9:24
text:
He covereth the faces of the judges thereof; he makes its judges blind to truth and justice, so that the cause of the innocent does not prevail with them. 
 
  If not, where, and who is he? if you say, It is not God who does this, then where and who is the ruler of the world? 
 
While God is never the author of sin, his hand is to be reverently acknowledged in all the evil that comes upon us through the agency of wicked men.

title: Job 9:25
text: A post; a runner sent, after the ancient custom, to carry a message.

title: Job 9:27
text: There is no help for man but in the grace of God, abounding through Jesus Christ our Lord.

title: Job 9:28
text:
Afraid of all my sorrows; terrified at the thought of the repeated calamities which God sends upon me. 
 
  I know that thou wilt not hold me innocent; the most distressing part of Job's trial was the despairing view which he took of God's dealings with him.  He felt that his Maker was determined to destroy him, and that there was no hope of any return of his former prosperity. In this the agency of Satan is clearly visible, and it must be taken into account if we would rightly interpret his vehement expressions of dismay and despondency. 
 
It is above all things important that the afflicted and tempted believer should avoid despairing views of the end of God's dealings with him; for nothing can so cut the sinews of his spiritual strength, and give Satan such an advantage over him.

title: Job 9:29
text: Why then labor I in vain? why should he seek to show that he was innocent when God would show him to be wicked?

title: Job 9:32
text:
Not a man, as I am; one with whom I can argue my cause on equal terms. 
 
  Answer him; contend with him in judgment, and try to show my innocence.

title: Job 9:33
text: Daysman; arbiter to decide between us.

title: Job 9:35
text: But it is not so with me; better, "for I am not so with myself;" that is, so conscious of being an ungodly man as to fear the result.

title: Job 10:1
text:
Leave my complaint; or, let loose my complaint; pour it out upon myself without restraint. 
 
Complaints under trials reflect on the wisdom and goodness of God, and unfit the soul to look unto him for help.

title: Job 10:2
text: Show me wherefore thou contendest with me; Job wished to know why it was that God so afflicted him.

title: Job 10:3
text: Shine upon the counsel of the wicked; by prospering them, and so afflicting Job as to give the wicked occasion to say he was a hypocrite.

title: Job 10:4
text:
vv 4-5. 
 
  Eyes of flesh--days of man; is God compelled, like man, to look on outward appearances? or is he, like man, short-lived and ignorant? These questions all have reference to  Job 10:6 .

title: Job 10:6
text: That thou inquirest--searchest; rather, that thou shouldest inquire and search.  Since thou art God, and not man, thou knowest me perfectly, without any necessity of long inquiry.

title: Job 10:7
text:
I am not wicked; not a hypocrite, as Satan and his agents contended.  Here he prays for deliverance from his sufferings on the ground of God's perfect knowledge of him as one of his upright worshippers. 
 
  There is none that can deliver; he asks for deliverance on the ground of God's absolute power and sovereignty, which enable Him to do all his pleasure. 
 
Conscious integrity is no sure safeguard against trials; nor will it, of itself, support the soul under them.  What is needed is the presence of the Holy Spirit, inspiring it with that confidence in God which is the substance of things hoped for, and the evidence of things not seen.

title: Job 10:8
text: Thy hands have made me; in this and the following verses he prays for deliverance on the ground that God is his maker, and has been hitherto his preserver.

title: Job 10:13
text: These things hast thou hid in thy heart; the reasons of Job's sufferings, as well as God's purposes concerning him, were all known to God, but not to him, and he was greatly perplexed in view of them.

title: Job 10:15
text:
If I be wicked; hypocritical, as his enemies said. 
 
  Righteous; upright, sincere, and pious, as he believed himself to be, notwithstanding all his troubles.

title: Job 10:16
text: Showest thyself marvellous upon me; inflictest upon me marvellous calamities.

title: Job 10:17
text: Without constant, strong, and loving confidence in God, trials may become so great, that even good men may wish to die, or find fault with God for bringing them into being, and continuing them amidst their accumulated sufferings.  But let them in patience wait upon God, and they will find that he is very pitiful and of tender mercy; that not a trial has been suffered that has not aided in working out for them an exceeding and eternal weight of glory.

title: Job 10:20
text: Cease then; cease to afflict me.

title: Job 10:21
text: The land of darkness; a description of the world of departed spirits, respecting which we must suppose Job had not the clear light which we now enjoy.

title: Job 11:3
text:
Lies; false assertions concerning his innocence and God's dealings with him. 
 
Men in controversy often charge their opponents with that of which they are not guilty; which tends only to irritate, not to convince; and which leads to personal altercation, rather than to an amicable adjustment of their differences.

title: Job 11:4
text:
My doctrine; here in the general sense of discourse concerning God and his dealings with men. 
 
  In thine eyes; in God's eyes.  Compare  Job 10:7 .

title: Job 11:6
text: That they are double to that which is; the word here translated "that which is," is often elsewhere rendered wisdom, or "counsel,"  Job 6:13 Job 12:16 Job 26:3 Proverbs 2:7 Proverbs 3:21 Proverbs 8:14 Isaiah 28:29 .  Retaining this meaning here, we may render the clause thus: "that there is double to counsel," meaning that God's counsel is double, or immensely great, far above and beyond what man can discover or understand.  Isaiah 40:2 Isaiah 61:7

title: Job 11:7
text: No one can fully understand the perfections of God, or the reasons of his ways; yet from revelation we can learn as much as it is needful for us to know, in order to be satisfied of his wisdom, justice, goodness, and truth.

title: Job 11:10
text:
Cut off; or, as the word is rendered in some other places, pass along, namely, for the purpose of apprehending or intercepting the sinner. 
 
  Shut up; against the day of trial. 
 
  Gather together; the people to witness the offender's trial.

title: Job 11:11
text:
He seeth wickedness; in men, often when they do not see it in themselves. 
 
The best human services are polluted in the sight of God; and the most perfect human characters need his pardoning mercy, through Jesus Christ.

title: Job 11:15
text: Spot; stain of sin or sorrow.

title: Job 11:17
text:
Thou shalt shine forth, thou shalt be as the morning; or, though thou be [now] in darkness, [then] thou shalt be as the morning. 
 
Light is sown for the righteous and gladness for the upright in heart. They may be afflicted here, and contrary to the doctrine of Zophar and his friends, their afflictions may continue to the end of life; but glory, honor, and perfect bliss await them in the life to come.

title: Job 11:18
text: Thou shalt dig; he might labor and rest in safety.  But some prefer to render, Though thou be [now] ashamed, [then] thou shalt rest in safety.

title: Job 12:2
text: Ye; Zophar and his friends; spoken in irony, meaning that they made vain pretentions.

title: Job 12:4
text: Who calleth--he answereth; or, who called--he answered.  I, who have been accustomed to call upon God, and receive answers from him, am now laughed to scorn.

title: Job 12:5
text:
Ready to slip; when a man falls into trouble, he is overlooked or treated with contempt by those who are in prosperity. 
 
  A lamp despised; a torch that is burned out, and therefore thrown away, as no longer of any service to the bearer. 
 
Men who are greatly courted and whose influence is eagerly sought in prosperity, are often overlooked and despised in adversity, and treated as if they were of no worth.

title: Job 12:6
text:
The tabernacles of robbers; very bad man are often prospered in this world, while very good men are afflicted. 
 
Though God is acquainted with all the wickedness of the wicked, and they are entirely dependent on him, yet in this world he often suffers them to prosper, and pours upon them abundance of earthly blessings.

title: Job 12:9
text:
In all these; in the proofs which all these classes of animals give of God's universal power and providence. 
 
  Hath wrought this; the whole course of nature and providence, in which is included the prosperity of the tabernacles of robbers,  Job 12:6 .

title: Job 12:11
text: The ear try words?--the mouth taste his meat? there is here an implied comparison: as the mouth can distinguish between savory and unsavory food, so the ear of a wise man can discern between wise and foolish words.

title: Job 12:12
text: With the ancient; with aged men, to whose wisdom I have access as well as you.

title: Job 12:13
text: Him; God.

title: Job 12:16
text: Are his; they are under his control, and all their circumstances directed by him.

title: Job 12:18
text:
Looseth the bond of kings; that is, according to our version, their authority over their subjects. 
 
  Girdeth their loins with a girdle; strengtheneth them for governing.  But many prefer to render, "He bindeth a band upon their loins."  The whole verse will then mean that he sets kings free from their bonds, and binds them at pleasure.

title: Job 12:20
text: The most wise and trustworthy of men, when left of God, wander in darkness; their wisdom is seen to be folly, and their plans come to naught.

title: Job 12:22
text: He discovereth deep things out of darkness; his infinite knowledge of all hidden things is here considered as enabling him to control the destinies of men.

title: Job 12:24
text: Taketh away the heart; leaves them to be infatuated, and to act without wisdom or discretion.

title: Job 13:1
text: All this; God's dealings, in his providence, with both the righteous and the wicked.

title: Job 13:3
text:
Reason with God; and not men, about the cause of my calamities. 
 
When the soul is conscious of integrity and duly feels its dependence on God, it will look to him, rather than to men for help, feeling that he alone can grant relief.

title: Job 13:4
text:
Forgers of lies; they gave a false view of the reasons of his afflictions. 
 
  Physcians of no value; they did not apply the right remedy to his case, nor in the least assuage his anguish.

title: Job 13:7
text: Speak wickedly for God; attempt to justify his ways by falsehood in respect to me.

title: Job 13:8
text: Will ye accept his person? show partiality towards him at the expense of truth and righteousness; as if he and his government needed to be defended by such means.

title: Job 13:9
text:
Is it good; will it result in your good? 
 
  Search you out; make manifest the unrighteousness of your proceedings under the pretence of honoring him. 
 
  Mock him; they mock God who defend his dealings towards men by falsehood and unjust accusations of their brethren. 
 
God does not need falsehood in his creatures to vindicate his dealings; and those who are guilty of it, whatever be their motives, will fall under his righteous displeasure.

title: Job 13:10
text: Secretly accept persons; see note to  Job 13:8 .

title: Job 13:12
text:
Remembrances; here probably in the sense of maxims of wisdom. 
 
  Your bodies to bodies of clay; or, your bulwarks are bulwarks of clay; that is, your boasted arguments amount to nothing.

title: Job 13:14
text: Take my flesh in my teeth; the same as, put my life in my hand; that is, expose myself to the loss of life by speaking boldly,  Job 13:13 .  The reason why he does this is, that he must speak, whatever shall be the result.

title: Job 13:15
text:
Maintain mine own ways; show his integrity, and that he was not a hypocrite. 
 
Confidence in God is the grand safeguard in trouble, and a preparation for deliverance from it.

title: Job 13:18
text: Shall be justified; proved to be innocent of the charges which they made against him.

title: Job 13:19
text: Who is he that will plead with me? a passionate expression of his desire to find one who understands his cause, and with whom he can argue it.  That one can be no other than God.

title: Job 13:20
text: Do not two things; continue not his distresses, nor overawe him with His majesty,  Job 13:21 .

title: Job 13:21
text: God can so afflict the soul and overawe it with his presence as entirely to unfit it to commune with him, or experience the benefit of calling upon him in spirit and in truth.

title: Job 13:23
text: Mine iniquities; for which he was so dreadfully afflicted.

title: Job 13:26
text:
Possess the iniquities of my youth; be punished for sins committed when young. 
 
Sins committed in early life may be the means of great sufferings in age, which shall continue till those who committed them go down to the grave.

title: Job 13:27
text: Puttest my feet--in the stocks; confined him by sickness as really as if put in the stocks.

title: Job 13:28
text: And he; man.  Here Job passes from the consideration of his own calamities to that of the common miseries of man.  See the following chapter.

title: Job 14:1
text: In this chapter Job laments the brevity and misery of human life.  The general course of thought is plain, and needs little illustration; yet  Job 14:13-15  presents peculiar difficulties.  The words in the preceding verse, "till the heavens be no more," may mean simply as long as the world stands.  Compare  Psalms 72:5 Psalms 72:17 , "they shall fear thee as long as the sun and moon endure;" "his name shall be continued as long as the sun."  Accordingly, some interpreters understand  Job 14:13-15  as expressing not so much Job's confident hope of what shall be, as his ardent wish what might be.  See notes to  Job 14:13-15 . Others think that in  Job 14:14-15 , he expresses the assurance that, though he die under the weight of his present trouble, he shall yet, when the period of his trial is past, see God interposing in his behalf, and rejoice in his salvation.  Thus understood,  Job 14:13-15  has a remarkable agreement with  Job 19:25-27 .  See notes to  Job 19:25-27 .

title: Job 14:2
text: The shortness and uncertainty of life should keep us from placing our affections on things below, and lead us to regard principally things unseen and eternal.

title: Job 14:4
text:
Not one; no one differs in natural moral character from his parents; but as are the parents, so are the children, naturally depraved and spiritually unclean. 
 
As children inherit the same depraved nature with their parents, they ought not to marvel at he change which Christ says they must experience, in order to see the kingdom of God.   John 3:3 f

title: Job 14:6
text: Rest; be freed for a little time from distresses.

title: Job 14:10
text:
Where is he? he does not appear again in this world; his departure is final. 
 
Earthly joys are uncertain, and at longest must be of short continuance; but the joys which await the people of God, when the heavens shall pass away with a great noise and the elements melt with fervent heat, will be sure, satisfying, and eternal.   II Peter 3:10

title: Job 14:13
text:
In the grave; literally, "in Sheol," the abode of departed spirits. 
 
  Wouldest appoint me a set time; namely, to bring me out of Sheol, again to enjoy thy favor.  Job was here led to pray for that very gift which God has in reserve for all who love him.

title: Job 14:14
text:
Shall he live again? that is, in this world.  The question is to be answered in the negative. 
 
  Appointed time; or, warfare, in the sense of exhausting sorrow,  Job 14:13 . 
 
  Will I wait; or, as we may also render, "would I wait."  So in the next verse we may translate, either, as in our version, "thou shalt call," or, "thou shouldest call," and so in the following clauses.

title: Job 14:16
text: For now thou numberest my steps; that thou mayest notice and punish any false step.

title: Job 14:17
text:
Sewest up mine iniquity; keepest it safe in thy record, till it shall be brought forth to judgment. 
 
The transgressions of the wicked are never forgotten; and unless repented of and forgiven through the atonement of Jesus Christ, will be brought forth to their shame and condemnation.

title: Job 14:19
text: The hope of man; his hope of continuing in this world.

title: Job 14:21
text: All that is done for our own welfare or that of others, must be done in time.  What our hands find to do, we should do with our might; that when our days on earth shall be finished, our work may be done, and our souls fitted, through grace, to enter on the rest which remains for the people of God.

title: Job 15:2
text: Utter vain knowledge; this Eliphaz ascribes to Job.

title: Job 15:4
text:
Fear; the fear of God.  This charge was unfounded. 
 
Those doctrines which lead men to cast off the fear of God and restrain prayer, must be false.

title: Job 15:5
text: The tongue of the crafty; by trying to cover his hypocrisy with the appearance of piety.

title: Job 15:6
text:
Thine own mouth condemneth thee; Eliphaz says that Job maintained doctrines which condemned himself, and showed that he was a hypocrite. 
 
The sentiments which many profess and propagate condemn themselves, and show them to be wicked men, as really as if they were guilty of open immorality.

title: Job 15:11
text: The consolations of God; those which Eliphaz and his friends offered as if they came from God.

title: Job 15:12
text:
Carry thee away; into such irreverent complaints against God. 
 
  What do thine eyes wink at; or, why do thine eyes wink?  Winking is here the gesture of anger and impatience.  Compare  Job 5:2 .

title: Job 15:13
text: Good men are sometimes liable to think that what is opposed to them, is opposed also to God; and thus unjustly charge others with opposition to him.

title: Job 15:19
text:
The earth; here in a restricted sense of the country where these ancients dwelt. 
 
  No stranger passed among them; they were not visited or corrupted by foreigners.

title: Job 15:20
text:
Is hidden; he knows not what is before him, or how soon or suddenly he may be cut off. 
 
The general and sweeping declarations of earnest disputants, while they express some important truth, may also express much hurtful error; and the true must be separated from the false, before their statements can safely be received.

title: Job 15:26
text:
He runneth upon--his bucklers; the whole verse may be thus rendered: "He [the wicked man] runneth upon him [God] with [proud] neck, with the thick bosses of his bucklers."  The wicked man is here compared to an armed warrior at the head of his band rushing upon God, his adversary. 
 
  His bucklers are the bucklers of his followers whom he leads forth to this impious war.

title: Job 15:27
text:
Covereth his face with his fatness; by pampering his appetite. 
 
  Callops; thick lumps.

title: Job 15:28
text: He dwelleth; or shall dwell.  This verse is interpreted in two different ways; either as describing the wicked man's violence, he dwelleth in cities made desolate by himself, etc,; or as describing his punishment, he shall, as an outcast from society, dwell in desolate cities, etc.  The latter is the more probable meaning.

title: Job 15:29
text:
Not be rich; not continue to be rich.  His blessings shall be short-lived. 
 
Though the wicked may be greatly prospered for a time, and in some instances their outward blessings be continued to the end of life, yet, if they continue in their wickedness, they are destined to poverty, shame, and everlasting contempt.

title: Job 15:30
text: By the breath of his mouth; by the angry breath of God.

title: Job 15:31
text:
In vanity; vanity here describes the wicked man's plans as empty, because destitute of righteousness and faith in God.
